title: The wind
hookLine: on a freezing night of the siege, Hudhayfah crosses to the enemy camp, holds his arrow, and the wind scatters the confederate armies (33:9; Muslim)

lines: A BITTER NIGHT OF THE SIEGE.
cards: Who will go and bring me news of the enemy? The Prophet Muhammad ﷺ asks it of his companions on a bitter night of the siege. The trench has held, but the armies are still camped beyond it.
Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman remembers this night in Sahih Muslim. No one answers. The Prophet asks again.
Silence. He asks a third time. Still no one stands up.

teach.b: Then the Prophet calls one man by name: get up, Hudhayfah. Once he was named, Hudhayfah says, he had no choice.
The Prophet gives him two instructions: bring me news of them, and don't stir them up against me. So he goes, alone, across the dark.
The strange part of his telling: on the way, he felt as if he were walking in a warm bath. He reaches the enemy camp and sees Abu Sufyan, the Meccan commander, warming his back at a fire.
Hudhayfah fits an arrow to his bow. He says he would have hit him. Then he remembers: don't stir them up.
He walks back, still warm, and gives his report, and the moment he's done, the cold comes back.

The Prophet wraps him in a spare cloak he used for prayer, and Hudhayfah sleeps there until morning, when the Prophet wakes him: get up, sleeper. Meanwhile, the camp he had walked through was coming apart.

teach.h: A GREAT WIND AND HOSTS YE COULD NOT SEE.
teach.b: Surah al-Ahzab remembers it in Pickthall's words: "O ye who believe! Remember Allah's favour unto you when there came against you hosts, and We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see."
The biographers say the wind knocked over pots and blew out fires, and the armies packed up and left. In Bukhari, the Prophet says afterward: now we will go to them, and they will not come to us.
Notice what Hudhayfah did not do. The one dramatic act within his reach, he held back.
In the Qur'an's telling, the ending came from the wind.

how: Muslims recite the opening of the Confederates passage, 33:9 onward, as a reminder of rescue under siege, and the phrase hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil is said by some in hard times.

o: the breath of a prophet, carrying his words far
the storm the Qur'an says broke up the armies
a desert sandstorm that hid the Muslims' retreat

p: sent alone to the enemy camp
warming his back at a fire
how the Prophet ﷺ woke him

s: many companions volunteered to go into the enemy camp
the Prophet asked again and again, and no one answered, until he named Hudhayfah.
Hudhayfah could have shot Abu Sufyan
he says he had an arrow on his bow and would have hit him, but remembered: don't stir them up.
33:9 says the armies were turned back by the trench alone
it says: We sent against them a great wind and hosts ye could not see.

games.q: you're Hudhayfah, alone in the enemy camp at night. the Meccan commander is warming himself at a fire, within range. what do you do?
o: shoot; this could end the siege.
lower the bow and go back with your report.
shout a warning so they know you were there.
games.why: he wanted to shoot, but remembered the Prophet's order: don't stir them up. he lowered the bow. the wind ended the siege.

practice: Think of something you're under siege from right now, a conflict, a worry, a long wait, and notice the arrow in your hand: the angry email, the sharp word, the move that would feel good for one second and stir everything up.

Hold it, the way Hudhayfah held his, and wait. If you pray, you can recite hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil, Allah is enough for us, and the best guardian, the words of 3:173; if not, let the storm be the storm.

wordCard.voice: The wind: the great wind of Surah al-Ahzab that broke up the armies around Medina, on the night Hudhayfah held his arrow. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: wind; the Qur'an uses the word in 33:9 for the wind sent against the confederate armies.

carryVoice: Your line: the wind came. The arrow stayed in his hand, and the ending came anyway. Until tomorrow.
